title: Callum and the Clock Tower Scale
markdown:
Callum loved to build. Not cardboard-box contraptions. Models. His current dream: the old clock tower in the centre of town, a giant model, perfectly to scale.

He had gathered wood, plastic, metal bits, even a tiny working clock mechanism no bigger than a thumbnail. In the workshop he suddenly felt quite small. The empty floor stretched. The tower in his mind seemed impossibly distant. A wobbly fluttery feeling in his tummy. “It’s just too big.” How to make every brick, window, gargoyle the right size when the whole thing had to be so very large? First attempts: a hundred tiny bricks for the base, then a hundred more. His head spun.

A rustle in the wood shavings. Fern the hedgehog, eyes like polished acorns. “What’s all this huffing? You look like you’ve swallowed a bumblebee.”

He pointed a shaky finger at a sprawling blueprint. “I want to build this. Impossible. Every part just right. So many parts. Too much to remember, too much to measure. I don’t know where to begin making it look like the real tower, only much bigger.”

Fern tilted her head, quills shivering. “You’re measuring everything at once. Start with one thing.” She scampered to a discarded piece of wood the size of a large book. “Make this, say, exactly one hundred times smaller than a real brick. Measure this one piece perfectly. Then everything else is measured by this piece, same scale. One hundred times smaller. Consistent. Like a matched pair of socks.”

A spark, a firefly on a dark leaf. He looked at the wood, then the drawings. One hundred times smaller. A tiny perfect snapshot of the whole, then made as big as needed without losing the relations. Scale. The immense tower felt… manageable.

He picked up fresh balsa. Measured, cut, sanded, until he had a single miniature brick, exactly one hundred times smaller than one from the real tower. The first one was a hair long; he sanded it again, because a wrong unit would multiply into a leaning town. Then another block, and another, each the same proportion. A small section of base, a tiny wall, a perfect miniature window frame, all to that one consistent scale. Fern’s paws were surprisingly steady holding pieces. She found the tiniest dropped screws against the shavings and once a gargoyle’s nose he had given up for lost.

As the sections grew, so did his confidence. The model rose, not with haphazard guessing, but ordered precision. Dr. Ada Brook entered, tweed coat swishing. She surveyed the work, eyes crinkling.

“Callum.” Warm as a winter fire, no dear attached. “Scale and proportion. Every measurement related to every other by a constant ratio. From a brick to a spire. A giant model relies on consistent scaling. One essential measure. Let it guide you.”

He beamed. The wobbly tummy had gone, replaced by something sturdy. The growing model was a clever idea, hedgehog wisdom, and perseverance.

No grandfather asked what happened next or what else worked that way. Callum glued the thumbnail clock into the miniature lantern, set Fern on the spire so she could claim she had invented height, and wrote 1:100 on the workshop wall in pencil, a number large enough to see from the door and small enough to keep.
